newsitem.title: CHINA: TRADE OFFICIAL SAYS FDI INFLOW NO THREAT TO CHINA.
newsitem.headline: TRADE OFFICIAL SAYS FDI INFLOW NO THREAT TO CHINA.

text.p: A flood of foreign direct investment (FDI) into China is no threat to its economic sovereignty and Beijing should not impose investment ceilings, the China Daily Business Weekly said.

However, China does need to prevent the development of monopolies by foreign investors, the newspaper said on Sunday quoting Liu Su, an official of the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation.
"It's high time to clear our entrenched fear that foreign direct investment might scuttle national economic autonomy," it quoted Liu as saying.
China should not try to protect its industry through non-economic measures but develop it through competition, Liu said.
Foreign investors "should not be taken as demons or devils", Liu said.
Foreign competition could help to promote economic efficiency, he added.
Liu dismissed concerns among some managers of domestic enterprises who fear their market share will be cut or remain stagnant as foreign investment pours into China.

Most Chinese managers believed their firms would retain or increase market share after China joins the World Trade Organisation, thus expanding market access to foreigners, he said citing a 1996 report by a research unit of the State Council, or cabinet.

Liu said foreign direct investment was superior as a source of funding to domestic investment and international loans because it also introduced advanced technology, modern market systems, and worldwide sales networks.
Foreign investment would also help China with its public infrastructure investment needs, estimated by the World Bank at $744 billion from 1995 to 2004, he said.
China approved 9,763 foreign-invested enterprises in the first half of 1997, with total contracted investment of $23.3 billion, down 48.76 percent year-on-year.
Actual foreign investment rose a year-on-year 5.35 percent in the first half to $20.721 billion.

China has been the world's second-largest user of foreign direct investment for the last four years, Liu said and issued a call to beware of attempts to turn China back from the open-door policy launched by the late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping nearly two decades ago.
"We should guard against attempts to turn China back into the old centrally planned system under the veneer of protecting national industry," he said.
However, another state newspaper said Beijing was mulling restrictions on foreign investment to reduce duplication and protect key national industries.

China would revise foreign investment regulations and transfer the right to approve investment in key industries that could easily be monopolised by foreign firms from provincial governments to the central government, the Wen Hui Bao said.
Some provincial governments were still blindly introducing foreign investment, resulting in duplication, wasted resources and an outflow of state assets, the newspaper said.
